claim: The read record says a body was sent, never that a body reached the agent. Four boundaries between the read command and the agent can eat a body. The record counts the first three as read. Two of those three say nothing an agent would read as a failure, and the third names an amount of output rather than a lost body. The fourth is the only one silent on both sides: the body reached the agent and no record was written at all.

evidence:
Measured 2026-09-02 across three agents on one checkout. `reading.module.ts:119` already names the gap: nothing is in the record that did not reach the agent.

First boundary: the read command's own 28000-byte answer. The command names the files left undelivered and hands back the exact next call, so recovery is possible. This boundary is the honest one.

Second boundary: an `akasha read` and an `akasha edit` chained into one shell call. About 20000 characters went missing from the middle of the read with no marker at all, while the record counted every file. The write then landed on bodies nobody held.

Third boundary: the harness answered `Output too large (44.8KB). Full output saved to <path>` with a 2KB preview. Four module pages were counted as read and no body reached the agent. Commit `a2118713a3` landed that way, and the debt was paid afterward with the change already in.

Both agents who met the third boundary read the marker as a note about output size rather than as the gate going blind. The rule an agent can act on: any message about output size near an `akasha read` is a read failure whatever the message calls the failure.

Fourth boundary, measured 2026-09-13 and since mended. A subagent's record file is found by looking its agent id up in the subagent page index, and that page is landed by a detached run the subagent does not wait for, so every read a subagent made before its page landed printed a whole body and recorded nothing. Landing latency measured over six subagents on one busy checkout: 9.1s, 11.6s, 12.8s, 14.7s, 15.2s, 15.8s. That is several agent turns, so an agent lost two or three calls to byte-identical output before one stuck, and read the repetition as the gate working. This is the only boundary silent on both sides: the first three lose the body and count it read, this one delivers the body and counts nothing. It failed safe for writes, an empty record refusing the write. `akasha read` now waits up to 60 seconds for the agent's own page, going the moment it lands and refusing with no body where it never does.

Two lists look alike and are not. The read's trailing `N files were left unread here` is the read's own output cap and never settles. The refused write's own list is the debt. Chasing the read's list went 19, 53, 31, 17. Taking the write's list went 19, 3, 1.
